title: Same Pattern of Letters
statement:
Two texts of the **same length** are **isomorphic** if the letters of `first` can be replaced by letters to give `second`, where every letter is always replaced by the same letter and **two different letters never get the same replacement**. A letter may be replaced by itself.

Return `true` if `first` and `second` are isomorphic, otherwise `false`.
constraints: both texts use only lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: p->t, a->i, e->l, r->e: every letter has one replacement and no two letters share one.
a and b would both have to become a, so two different letters share a replacement.

hints.nudge: The rule has two directions: one letter must not need two different replacements, and two letters must not share one replacement. What do you need to remember to check both?
hints.pattern: Two hash maps (first -> second and second -> first), checked at every position.
hints.pseudocode:
forward = {}; backward = {}
for i in 0..n-1:
  a = first[i]; b = second[i]
  if a in forward and forward[a] != b: return false
  if b in backward and backward[b] != a: return false
  forward[a] = b; backward[b] = a
return true
hints.walkthrough: Walk through both texts together. The map `forward` remembers which letter each letter of `first` has been paired with; if a letter shows up again with a different partner, the first rule is broken. The map `backward` remembers which letter of `first` each letter of `second` was paired with; if a letter of `second` shows up again with a different partner, two different letters would share a replacement, which breaks the second rule. Checking only one direction is the classic mistake (it says `ab` and `aa` are isomorphic). Another trick: two texts are isomorphic exactly when the position of the FIRST occurrence of each letter gives the same list for both. O(n) time; the maps hold at most 26 letters.
